extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP attorneys, in-house counsel, and legal practitioners handling Korean patent disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and procedural standards for litigating patent and related IP disputes in the Republic of Korea, covering defenses, jurisdiction, case management, evidence, provisional remedies and required contents of briefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse-of-rights defense (lack of inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee’s claim for damages or injunction may constitute an abuse of rights and be impermissible when it is clear the patented invention lacks an inventive step and will be invalidated by an administrative invalidation proceeding; the court handling the infringement suit may review and determine inventive step to decide the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the clarity requirement is met when the judge finds the invention lacks an inventive step in the infringement suit. The defense is treated similarly where the patent lacks novelty or sufficient description. The plaintiff may reply by filing a correction to narrow claims or correct errors, provided the correction does not substantially alter what is claimed (can be done in IPTAB or separate correction petition). (Cited: Daebeobwon (Sup. Ct), Jan. 19, 2012, 2010Da95390.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-to-exploit-technology defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may argue their product/process only implements technology that was publicly known or easily derivable from public knowledge, so it does not fall within the patentee’s scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant’s product consists only of publicly known technologies or can be easily practiced by a person of ordinary skill from public technologies, comparison with the patent is unnecessary to conclude non-infringement. This analysis resembles inventive-step assessment but compares the defendant’s product with public knowledge rather than the patented invention. Rarely used in infringement suits because abuse-of-rights defenses (questioning inventive step) are often preferred. (Cited: Daebeobwon (Sup. Ct), Sep. 23, 2004.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Known-technology defense (public use/known at filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patented invention consists only of technologies already publicly known or in public use at the time of filing, the patentee may not exercise patent rights; the defendant bears the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense can be asserted alongside free-to-exploit arguments but is less frequently used than abuse-of-rights or free-to-exploit defenses. The defendant must provide contention and proof that the invention was publicly known. (Reference: scholarly commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent exhaustion (first sale) doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Resale or use of a lawfully transferred patented product generally does not constitute patent infringement; patent rights in the sold product are exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognized by the Supreme Court for product patents: when a patentee or licensee lawfully sells the product in Korea, the patent effects do not extend to acts of using, assigning or leasing that product by the assignee or buyer. (Cited: Daebeobwon (Sup. Ct), April 11, 2003.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited effect and lawful practice defenses (licenses, statutory/compulsory licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses that the effect of the patent is limited, or that the defendant has an exclusive/nonexclusive/license or a statutory or compulsory license under specified Patent Act provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant Patent Act provisions include Articles 96, 98, 103–107, 122, 138, 181, 182, 183 (statutory/compulsory licenses and limits). These are affirmative defenses a defendant may assert to justify exploiting the patented technology. (Scholarly reference: IP Litigation Research Committee.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory burden-shifting and evidentiary presumptions in patent litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act includes provisions that shift burdens or create rebuttable presumptions (e.g., presumption of manufacturing process, of negligence, acts deemed infringement) and special orders (disclosure, submission of materials, obligation to explain matters for appraisal) to ease patentees’ proof burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Article 127 (acts deemed infringement), Article 129 (presumption of manufacturing process), Article 130 (presumption of negligence), Article 126-2 (disclosure of actual product/process), Article 132 (order to submit materials), Article 128-2 (obligation to explain matters for appraisal). Courts balance these provisions with defendants’ rights; they are tools to address concentration of evidence with the defendant. (See text for full list and context.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Available civil remedies for patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may seek injunctions (preventing infringement), disposal/destruction of infringing means, recovery of reputation, compensatory damages, and restitution of unjust enrichment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent injunctions, disposal orders (Article 126(2)), and reputation recovery (Article 131) are available. Damages or restitution may be claimed for loss caused by infringement. Remedies may be sought together (e.g., injunction plus damages) and affect trial complexity and timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for employee invention compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee is entitled to fair compensation when an employer secures patents/utility models/design rights or exclusive licenses arising from the employee’s invention; employee may sue for compensation if they believe payment was unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights arise under Article 15(1) of the Invention Promotion Act; such claims often implicate patent, civil, and labor law cross-issues and may be brought as separate suits for compensation. (See Section referenced.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil action initiation and trial structure in Korea
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil patent action is initiated by filing a complaint in the district court with territorial jurisdiction (defendant's residence/place of business); service is by the court; trials occur as multiple short sessions spaced weeks apart rather than a single lengthy trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First trial usually 2–3 months after filing; patent trials are longer due to technical presentations. Typical timelines: injunction-only main action ~8–12 months; injunction plus damages ~12–18 months. Service by mail or other delivery; public notice service if defendant locations unknown. (Civil Procedure Act references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic Case Filing System (ECFS) usage and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: ECFS enables paperless filing and management of civil actions in the Korean judiciary, often used for patent cases and not mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features: e-filing of documents and evidence (including digital evidence), email/text notifications of filings, judges can view records electronically, files closed to public (only litigants/attorneys/court), published decisions accessible via judiciary online decision search. Adoption has largely replaced paper processes and improved case management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial jurisdiction and concentration for patent/other listed IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws concentrate jurisdiction for suits concerning patents and other listed IP rights to specific district courts (six district courts with concurrent jurisdiction to Seoul Central District Court) and prohibit parties from contracting around exclusive jurisdiction; Patent Court has exclusive appellate jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 24(2) Civil Procedure Act and Article 28-4 Court Organization Act establish exclusive jurisdiction and Patent Court appellate competence. ‘Patent and other listed IP rights’ are defined to include patent, utility model, trademark, design and plant variety rights; determining whether a suit 'concerns' those rights is critical to jurisdiction. Transfer rules apply if brought in wrong court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case transfer rules for jurisdictional defects
rubrics_metrics.description: A court lacking jurisdiction over a patent/listed IP rights lawsuit must transfer the case to a competent court; courts may transfer to avoid significant damage or delay when necessary (Article 36(3) Civil Procedure Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal interpretation suggests Article 36(3) may not apply to appeals, and there have been calls to allow discretionary transfers to courts of general appellate jurisdiction to prevent damage/delay. Parties cannot render a court competent by waiving jurisdictional defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction venue rules (territorial split)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions (provisional disposition) may be brought to any district court having jurisdiction over the location of the disputed subject matter, not limited to the exclusive IP jurisdiction courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 303 Civil Execution Act assigns jurisdiction to the court having jurisdiction over the merits or the district court over the location of the disputed subject matter. Appeals from preliminary injunctions go to the competent high court rather than the Patent Court (Patent Court appellate jurisdiction excludes such appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter jurisdiction (single judge vs panel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocation of first-instance adjudication between single judges and three-judge panels depends on subject matter: monetary claims exceeding KRW 500 million go to a three-judge panel, while KRW 500 million or less go to a single judge; certain claims (injunction, transfer/extinguishment of registration) are panel cases regardless of calculable value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value of the subject is calculated on the benefits claimed; joined claims are summed. Courts (e.g., Seoul Central District Court) may assign cases to panels by decision regardless of value. Statutory thresholds and Rules on Subject-Matter Jurisdiction govern these allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction and court levels in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Court has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over lawsuits concerning patents and other listed IP rights; Supreme Court is the court of last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For IP rights other than the listed ones, appeals follow usual routes (panel of district court or high court). Patent Court exclusivity applies irrespective of first-instance subject-matter jurisdiction (single judge vs panel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents and timing for briefs (statements of case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must submit written briefs in advance. New offensive/defensive methods must be filed in time to be served at least seven days before trial; briefs should be timely to allow opponent’s response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cautions: inventive-step contentions need element-by-element charts identifying prior-art elements and mapping to patented elements; for combined prior art, specify primary prior art and explain how others combine and why combination is obvious to a person of ordinary skill. Infringement contentions must list product name/type numbers, attach drawings/photos, and include element-by-element charts comparing accused product/process with the patent, described both individually and graphically. Damages claims must specify legal provisions used for calculation and identify exhibit numbers tied to each legal element. When disputing allegations, respond with detailed answers rather than simple denials. (Civil Procedure Act articles and court rules cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Early case management duties (judge-set trial date and triage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presiding judge must set trial dates without delay once answer filed and evaluate dispute intensity, complexity, suitability for mediation, and urgency to set the earliest practical trial date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If early mediation likely to settle case, judge may refer to mediation before first trial date. Early case management aims to streamline discovery, hearings, and overall schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory hearing functions and typical agenda items
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparatory hearings (held in exceptional/complex patent cases) sort arguments and evidence and coordinate case management, often via video conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common topics: trial date/timetable; deadlines for stating contentions and submitting evidence (comprehensive briefs, expert affidavits), maximum number and length of submissions; whether to use time-consuming evidence methods (inspection, appraisal, expert witnesses) and their deadlines; whether to designate a technical advisor; whether to hold technology review sessions; whether to hold separate hearings by legal issue (infringement, invalidity, damages); coordination with related IPTAB proceedings; referral to mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction standards and practical evidence expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions require plaintiff to show likelihood of infringement and necessity for provisional relief; courts balance irreparable harm to plaintiff against economic harm to defendant and consider adequacy of relief and likelihood of patent invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary injunctions are generally inter partes with mandatory hearings; initial hearing usually within 2–3 weeks of filing. Documentary evidence (brochures, product samples) and affidavits are primary because witnesses rarely testify in person. Very little discovery is allowed; courts reluctant to grant injunctions where expert testimony/tests are required. Plaintiffs should gather documentary evidence pre-filing. Courts may require security deposit; injunctions can be enforced while appeal pending. If injunction is improperly issued, the right holder may be liable for ordinary and foreseeable extraordinary damages and is rebuttably presumed negligent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures and consequences surrounding preliminary injunction orders
rubrics_metrics.description: When granting a preliminary injunction the court may prohibit manufacture/sale, order custody/transfer of infringing articles, or instruct posting notice; plaintiff usually must post security; improperly granted injunctions expose right holder to tort liability and presumed negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security deposit returns if injunction becomes final after appeals. Defendant can request reconsideration, appeal to the high court, or ask the court to compel the plaintiff to file the main suit within a deadline; failure to file main complaint can lead to revocation of the preliminary injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence production framework (no broad pre-trial discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean civil procedure lacks broad discovery mechanisms (depositions/interrogatories). Evidence is produced during trials; pre-filing preservation/examination is possible by petition to the court in exceptional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All requests for production are by petition; court exercises discretion balancing need for evidence against delay/harm. Any party submitting documentary evidence or seeking witness/orders must specify in detail the matters to be substantiated by that evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary evidence standards (originals, scans, translations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable documentary evidence includes patent specifications, technical literature, published materials, patent gazettes, product models, photos, videos; originals preferred but scanned copies acceptable unless authenticity is disputed; foreign-language documents must be submitted with translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the other party disputes the existence/authenticity of a scanned document, the original must be made available for examination at trial. Exception noted for permitted languages in international cases. Ensure exhibits are properly identified and linked to legal contentions (e.g., damages calculation exhibits).
